name: Germany
score_rationale: LAND stays 1: ownership is nationality-neutral but farmland averages USD 40,000/ha (USD 17,000 in the cheapest eastern states) and GrdstVG approval plus Landgesellschaft pre-emption can block non-farmer buyers. VISA stays 1: no passive-income, golden or nomad visa; retirees depend on discretionary section 7 permits and private insurance; the only group-friendly route is forming a farm business under section 21 or sponsoring skilled workers; citizenship 5 years with dual nationality allowed, but the 3-year fast track died in Oct 2025. TAX stays 1: worldwide taxation at 45 percent plus soli, no wealth tax, crypto 1-year exemption still live but slated for a 25 percent flat tax from 2027. LAW stays 2: the eG, Stiftung/Erbbaurecht and Mietshaeuser Syndikat models are the best communal vehicles in the atlas, but section 35 BauGB zoning denies new housing on open farmland, which caps the score. LIFE stays 3 (HDI 0.959, WJP 0.83, Numbeo QoL 200.85, universal healthcare). STAB stays 3 (FSI 24.0, CPI 77, ND-GAIN 3rd) despite the GPI slide from 20th to 28th in 2026.
verdict: Gold-standard co-op law and stability, but land is expensive, building is strict, and there's no easy passive-income visa.
summary: Germany has the world's most mature legal toolkit for communal land (the eingetragene Genossenschaft, Stiftung-plus-Erbbaurecht models like Stiftung trias, the Mietshaeuser Syndikat) and top-tier stability, but farmland averages EUR 35,300/ha (about USD 40,000; eastern states about EUR 15,000/ha), sales of farmland are subject to Grundstueckverkehrsgesetz approval that can favour local farmers, and you cannot build new housing on open farmland (section 35 BauGB) unless you are a bona fide farm business, so plan on buying an existing farmstead or village site. Non-EU members have no passive-income or golden visa: each person needs an individual basis (section 21 self-employment, Blue Card or skilled-worker permit, or a discretionary section 7 retiree permit) plus full health insurance; permanent residence takes 3 to 5 years and citizenship 5 years (the 3-year fast track was repealed on 30 Oct 2025). Taxation is worldwide at up to 45 percent plus 5.5 percent solidarity surcharge, with no wealth tax and crypto still tax-free after a one-year hold, though the government is drafting a 25 percent flat crypto tax for 2027.

land.text: East-German depopulation, but farmland pricey (~€26k/ha) & strict
land.house: Rare cheap-village stock in the east; no formal program
land.ownership_note: Nationality is irrelevant: EU and non-EU persons and foreign-owned companies can hold German farmland freehold on the same terms as Germans. The real constraint is structural, not national. Under the Grundstueckverkehrsgesetz (GrdstVG) every sale of agricultural or forestry land above a state-set threshold (0.15 ha in Saarland up to 2 ha in Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Saxony-Anhalt and Schleswig-Holstein; Baden-Wuerttemberg has its own ASVG) needs approval from the agricultural authority, which can be refused under section 9 GrdstVG for an 'ungesunde Verteilung des Grund und Bodens' (typically a sale to a non-farmer when a local full-time farmer needs the land), an uneconomic split (agricultural parcels below 1 ha, forest below 3.5 ha) or a price grossly above market value. For parcels of 2 ha or more the non-profit Landgesellschaft holds a statutory pre-emption right under section 4 Reichssiedlungsgesetz when approval would otherwise be refused. A group that registers as a farm business (eG or GmbH actually farming the land) is treated as a farmer for these purposes; buying an existing farmstead with buildings (Hofstelle) or leasing (Pacht; arable rents average roughly EUR 400/ha/yr) are the common workarounds. Prices (Destatis 2024): national average EUR 35,300/ha for all agricultural land, arable EUR 42,800, grassland EUR 24,800; West EUR 53,500 vs East EUR 16,800; cheapest states Brandenburg EUR 14,915, Thuringia EUR 14,926, Saarland EUR 15,042, Saxony EUR 17,789; dearest North Rhine-Westphalia EUR 97,727 and Bavaria EUR 94,415.
land.build_rules: GrdstVG section 9 presumes an uneconomic split if an agricultural parcel would fall below 1 ha or forest below 3.5 ha, so micro-parcelling land among members can be refused. New dwellings in the Aussenbereich (outside the built-up area or a Bebauungsplan) are only permitted under section 35(1) BauGB if they 'serve' an agricultural or forestry business and occupy a subordinate part of its land; section 35(4) allows conversion of preserved farm buildings into at most 5 additional dwellings per farmstead if the exterior is kept and the building was not abandoned more than 7 years.
land.cheap_house_program: None. There is no national or state 'one-euro house' scheme. Cheap village stock exists in depopulating eastern districts (Brandenburg, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern) where whole farmsteads and manor complexes (e.g. Schloss Tonndorf 2005, Hof Praedikow 2016) were bought by groups, but each is an ordinary private purchase subject to GrdstVG approval and real-estate transfer tax of 3.5 to 6.5 percent.
land.note: Land is expensive by global standards but the East-West gap is huge: USD 17,000/ha in Brandenburg or Thuringia vs USD 110,000/ha in NRW. Rents are a cheaper entry (arable rents about EUR 400/ha/yr) and long-term Pacht contracts are standard. Property purchase also triggers Grunderwerbsteuer (3.5 to 6.5 percent) and notary/registry fees; Grundsteuer (annual property tax) was re-based from 1 Jan 2025.

visas.name: Residence permit for self-employment / entrepreneur (section 21(1) AufenthG)
visas.requirement: A business plan showing (1) an economic interest or regional need, (2) expected positive effects on the economy, and (3) secured financing via own capital or a loan commitment; no statutory minimum capital or job count since the 2012 reform of section 21. Applicants over 45 must show adequate old-age provision (section 21(3)). A registered farm business or eco-village enterprise (eG/GmbH) can be the vehicle for several founding members. Practical livelihood proof of roughly EUR 2,000 to 2,500 net per month per adult is expected by most missions.
visas.initial_term: Up to 3 years (section 21(4)), renewable while the business is viable
visas.processing_time: Typically 6 to 12 weeks at the embassy, up to 3 to 6 months in slow missions; the embassy must decide within 3 months (section 75 VwGO)

visas.name: Freelancer residence permit (section 21(5) AufenthG, Freiberufler)
visas.requirement: Liberal profession (artists, writers, IT consultants, teachers, architects, physicians etc.) with any licence required; proof of clients/contracts and income sufficient to live without public funds, in practice about EUR 2,000 to 2,500 net per month in cities, less in rural areas; proof of health insurance; over-45s show pension provision. Note: the 3-year settlement path of section 21(4) does NOT apply to freelancers; they go through the general 5-year rule of section 9.
visas.initial_term: 1 to 3 years, renewable
visas.processing_time: 6 to 12 weeks typical; 60 to 180 days depending on consulate

visas.name: EU Blue Card (section 18g AufenthG)
visas.requirement: Recognised university degree plus a job offer of at least 6 months paying at least EUR 50,700 gross per year in 2026 (EUR 45,934.20 for shortage occupations such as IT, engineering, medicine, and for graduates within 3 years of their degree). Thresholds are 50 percent / 45.3 percent of the pension contribution ceiling (EUR 101,400 in 2026) and reset every January.
visas.initial_term: Up to 4 years (or contract length plus 3 months)
visas.processing_time: 4 to 12 weeks; accelerated procedure available via employer

visas.name: Skilled worker residence permit (sections 18a/18b AufenthG) with settlement under section 18c
visas.requirement: Recognised vocational or academic qualification plus a concrete job offer in Germany (agricultural employers can sponsor, e.g. an organic farm or eco-village enterprise); Federal Employment Agency consent; secured livelihood. Settlement permit after 36 months of residence permit and pension contributions (24 months if trained in Germany) with sufficient German; Blue Card holders after 27 months or 21 months with B1 German.
visas.initial_term: Up to 4 years

visas.name: Opportunity Card / Chancenkarte (section 20a AufenthG, job-search permit, since June 2024)
visas.requirement: Either a fully recognised foreign qualification, or at least 6 points under the points system plus a state-recognised vocational qualification of at least 2 years or a degree and at least A1 German or B2 English; livelihood must be secured (blocked account at the standard rate set by the authorities; verify the current monthly figure with the embassy). Allows part-time work of at most 20 hours per week on average and 2-week trial jobs; converts to a skilled-worker or Blue Card permit once a qualified job is found; extendable by up to 2 years only if a qualified job contract is obtained.
visas.initial_term: Up to 1 year

visas.name: Retiree / person of independent means residence permit (section 7(1) sentence 3 AufenthG, discretionary)
visas.requirement: No dedicated retirement visa exists; section 7(1) s.3 lets the Auslaenderbehoerde grant a permit 'in begruendeten Faellen' for a purpose not listed in the Act. No statutory income floor: authorities expect passive income or assets clearly above the subsistence level, in practice at least about EUR 1,200 to 1,500 per month plus rent, full German-standard health insurance (third-country retirees usually cannot join statutory GKV and must buy private cover; applicants over roughly 75 may be refused by insurers), adequate housing and ties to Germany. Grant is discretionary and varies by district; retirees in rural depopulating districts often get a friendlier hearing. Permanent settlement after 5 years under section 9 requires 60 months of statutory pension contributions or comparable private provision, B1 German and civic knowledge.
visas.initial_term: 1 year, renewable (typically 1 to 2 years per renewal)
visas.processing_time: 2 to 4 months at the embassy; several months at local offices

visas.name: Digital nomad visa
visas.requirement: Germany has no digital-nomad visa. Remote workers must use the freelancer permit (section 21(5)) with German clients or a German business footprint, the Chancenkarte, or a skilled-worker route; remote employment for a foreign employer alone is not a recognised purpose of residence. EU/EEA/Swiss citizens need no permit at all.
visas.initial_term: n/a

visas.name: Restoration of citizenship for descendants of Nazi-era persecution (Art. 116(2) Basic Law and section 15 StAG) and declaration route (section 5 StAG)
visas.requirement: Descendants of persons deprived of German citizenship on political, racial or religious grounds between 30 Jan 1933 and 8 May 1945 (and, under section 15 StAG, of those who were excluded from acquiring it) can claim German citizenship by declaration with no residence, language or renunciation requirement. Section 5 StAG also lets children born before 1 Jan 2000 to a German parent who could not pass on citizenship under old gender-discriminatory rules (and their descendants) acquire citizenship by declaration until 19 Aug 2031. German citizens are EU citizens with full settlement and work rights.
visas.initial_term: Citizenship outright (no permit)
visas.processing_time: Typically 1 to 3 years at the Bundesverwaltungsamt

visa_text: Freelancer/self-employ, skilled-worker; citizenship now 5y
visa_detail: Freelancer/self-employed or skilled-worker visa; income-proof. ~1–3 mo. Settlement ~5 yr (fast-track 3) · citizenship now 5 yr.
visa_note: EU/EEA/Swiss citizens simply register (Anmeldung) and can buy land and farm immediately. For third-country members there is no passive-income, rentista, golden or digital-nomad visa and no investor minimum; the realistic group strategy is to form the farm/eco-village enterprise first (eG or GmbH) and bring founders in under section 21(1) (settlement after 3 years) and employees under skilled-worker/Blue Card permits (settlement after 21 to 36 months), with retirees on discretionary section 7 permits. Since the Staatsangehoerigkeitsmodernisierungsgesetz of 27 June 2024, naturalisation needs 5 years of lawful residence, B1 German, secured livelihood and a civics test, and dual citizenship is allowed; the 3-year fast track for 'special integration' was repealed with effect from 30 Oct 2025 (Bundestag vote 8 Oct 2025, 450 to 134). Spouses of Germans still qualify after 3 years. Processing is slow at many Auslaenderbehoerden (months) even when embassy decisions are fast.

tax.text: Income to 45%; no wealth tax; crypto 0% after 1yr hold
tax.capital_gains: Investment income (interest, dividends, gains on securities) is taxed at a flat 25 percent plus 5.5 percent solidarity surcharge = 26.375 percent (plus church tax if a member), withheld at source, with a EUR 1,000 saver's allowance per person (EUR 2,000 for couples). Private sale transactions: movable assets including crypto are tax-free if held more than 1 year, otherwise taxed at the progressive rate; gains are exempt if total private-sale gains in the year are under EUR 1,000. Real estate is tax-free after a 10-year holding period (or if owner-occupied in the year of sale and the two prior years).
tax.wealth_tax: None (suspended since 1997). Inheritance and gift tax is progressive at 7 to 50 percent with allowances of EUR 20,000 to 500,000 depending on relationship; transfers of business and agricultural assets enjoy substantial relief.
tax.property_tax: Grundsteuer (annual, municipal) was re-based from 1 Jan 2025 under the new valuation law (federal model or state variants); amounts are modest for rural land and houses but depend on the municipal Hebesatz. Grundsteuer A applies to agricultural land. Real estate transfer tax (Grunderwerbsteuer) of 3.5 to 6.5 percent of the price is due on every purchase, varying by state.
tax.foreign_pension: German tax residents are taxed on worldwide pension income. Under the US-Germany treaty US Social Security paid to a German resident is taxable only in Germany (Art. 18(5)); private pensions, IRAs and 401(k) distributions are taxable in the residence state (Art. 18/18A); government-service pensions stay taxable in the paying state (Art. 19). From the 2025 assessment period, foreign pensions whose contributions were tax-privileged abroad are fully taxable in Germany (confirmed by the Federal Fiscal Court for US plans). UK state and public-service pensions follow the UK-Germany treaty. No special low-tax regime for inbound retirees exists.
tax.special_regime: No inbound flat-tax, non-dom or lump-sum regime. Solidarity surcharge of 5.5 percent on income tax applies only above an income-tax burden of about EUR 19,950 (single) / 39,900 (joint); church tax 8 to 9 percent of income tax if registered as a member. Married couples can split income (Ehegattensplitting). Top rate 45 percent applies above EUR 277,826 taxable income (2025); the 42 percent band starts at EUR 68,430.
tax.crypto: Private crypto gains are tax-free after a holding period of more than 12 months (section 23 EStG one-year rule), otherwise taxed at progressive rates up to 45 percent with a EUR 1,000 annual exemption. Flag for 2027: a federal cabinet position adopted in July 2026 points to moving crypto gains into the 25 percent flat investment-income regime from 2027 (effective 26.375 percent with soli); as of 10 Sep 2026 no statutory text had been published and the one-year exemption remains in force.
tax.coop_treatment: An eingetragene Genossenschaft is a corporation taxed at 15 percent corporate tax plus 5.5 percent soli and municipal trade tax, but section 5(1) no. 14 KStG fully exempts agricultural and forestry cooperatives and associations whose activities are confined to shared use of farm equipment, services, processing or marketing of members' own agricultural products (non-member/other revenue must stay at or below 10 percent of total). Bodies recognised as gemeinnuetzig (charitable, e.g. an e.V., gGmbH or Stiftung for education/ecology) are exempt under section 5(1) no. 9 KStG and can issue donation receipts.

cost.note: About EUR 1,300 to 1,700 per adult per month in a small town or village (2026 prices): rent EUR 400 to 800 for a one-bedroom outside city centres (far less, or zero, when living on a bought farmstead), groceries EUR 200 to 300, utilities EUR 150 to 200, health insurance from about EUR 270 per month for a self-employed person on the minimum assessment base (private cover averages about EUR 520), transport EUR 60 to 100 for a pass or EUR 170 to 350 with a car. National single-person averages are EUR 1,800 to 2,500 including big-city rents; Saarbruecken-type small cities run roughly 40 percent below Munich.

health.system: Bismarck-model dual system: statutory health insurance (GKV, about 90 percent of residents, income-based premiums, family members co-insured free) alongside substitutive private insurance (PKV, risk-rated premiums). Insurance is compulsory for every resident from day one, and proof of cover is a condition of every residence permit.
health.cost_for_residents: GKV 2026: 14.6 percent (14.0 percent without sick-pay entitlement) plus an insurer-specific supplementary contribution averaging 2.9 percent plus 3.6 percent long-term care (4.2 percent if childless over 23), i.e. about 21 percent of income; employees split this with the employer, the self-employed pay all of it on a minimum assessment base of EUR 1,316.67/month (minimum premium about EUR 270/month) up to the ceiling of EUR 5,812.50/month (maximum about EUR 1,200/month). Private cover averages about EUR 520/month and rises with age. Out-of-pocket co-pays are small (EUR 10 per prescription, capped at 2 percent of income).
health.immigrant_access: Employees are enrolled in GKV automatically. Self-employed arrivals can join GKV voluntarily only if they move their permanent residence to Germany, register the activity, and apply within 3 months of leaving a prior (EU/EEA/treaty-state or German) insurance; otherwise they must take PKV or an expat policy. Third-country retirees and passive-income holders usually cannot enter GKV and must buy private cover that meets section 193 VVG standards; insurers may refuse applicants over about 75 or with pre-existing conditions, which can block the section 7 retiree permit. Once in, access to care is identical to citizens.
health.quality_note: Dense rural GP and hospital network, though rural GP shortages are growing in the east; HDI life expectancy 81.4 years; Numbeo healthcare index 71.25 (Oct 2026).

pension.foreign_pension_tax: Taxed as ordinary income at progressive rates up to 45 percent plus soli once resident; US Social Security and private pensions are taxable only in Germany under the US-Germany treaty (Art. 18(5), 18/18A), government-service pensions only in the paying state (Art. 19); since the 2025 assessment period foreign pensions built from tax-privileged contributions are 100 percent taxable (BFH ruling on US plans). No remittance or flat-rate concession for foreign retirees; the basic allowance is EUR 12,096 (2025).
pension.retiree_visa: None dedicated. Retirees apply under the discretionary section 7(1) sentence 3 AufenthG 'other purpose' permit: show passive income/assets comfortably above subsistence (in practice about EUR 1,200 to 1,500/month plus rent), private health insurance meeting German standards, and housing; 1-year renewable permits, no work; permanent residence after 5 years under section 9 requires 60 months of statutory pension contributions or comparable private provision plus B1 German, which many retirees never satisfy. Processing 2 to 4 months at the embassy.

ag.subsidies: EU CAP 2023-2027 direct payments (GAP-Direktzahlungen) are open to any active farmer with eligible land, regardless of nationality or legal form. 2025 unit rates: basic income support (Einkommensgrundstuetzung) EUR 152.44/ha; redistributive top-up EUR 68.05/ha for the first 40 ha and EUR 40.83/ha for ha 41-60 (favours small farms); young-farmer top-up EUR 120.64/ha for up to 120 ha for a maximum of 5 years (farmer under 41); voluntary eco-schemes (Oeko-Regelungen) EUR 40 to 1,300/ha depending on measure (e.g. non-productive arable set-aside, flower strips, agroforestry, organic). 2026 planned rates: EUR 147.38 basic, EUR 65.31/39.19 redistributive, EUR 134.04 young farmer. Second-pillar organic conversion and maintenance premiums and agri-environment payments are run by each Land. Applications go through the annual Gemeinsamer Antrag (deadline 15 May).
ag.coop_law: Genossenschaftsgesetz (GenG) of 1889, in force in its current version: section 1 defines the eingetragene Genossenschaft (eG) as a society of unlimited membership whose purpose is to promote members' economic interests or, since the 2006 amendment, their social or cultural concerns through a joint business; section 4 requires at least 3 members; the eG must belong to a cooperative auditing federation (Pruefungsverband). Agricultural eGs are corporate-tax exempt under section 5(1) no. 14 KStG if non-member business stays within 10 percent. Germany's Raiffeisen cooperative tradition dates to the 1860s and the Deutscher Raiffeisenverband federates thousands of agricultural cooperatives.
ag.equipment_note: Eco-scheme and agri-environment payments (EUR 40 to 1,300/ha) are the most accessible money for a small diversified farm; investment grants for buildings and machinery exist under the Laender's agricultural investment programmes within the GAK framework but require a full-time farm business plan and co-financing, so a new commune should budget on CAP area payments only until it qualifies as an established farm.

legal.text: Genossenschaft (very strong co-op law), eingetragener Verein, Stiftung

vehicles.name: Eingetragene Genossenschaft (eG) under the Genossenschaftsgesetz (GenG, 1889)
vehicles.note: The standard German commune vehicle: at least 3 members (section 4 GenG), one member one vote, open membership, may pursue economic, social or cultural purposes (section 1 GenG), limited liability, can own farmland and buildings and run the farm; mandatory membership in a Pruefungsverband with periodic audits adds cost but also credibility with banks. Used by Sieben Linden (Siedlungsgenossenschaft Oekodorf eG), Schloss Tempelhof eG, Schloss Tonndorf eG and SelbstBau eG at Hof Praedikow; agricultural eGs are corporate-tax exempt under section 5(1) no. 14 KStG.

vehicles.name: Eingetragener Verein (e.V.) under sections 21 ff. BGB
vehicles.note: Non-commercial association gaining legal personality by entry in the Vereinsregister (section 21 BGB); cheap, 7 founders customary, can hold land and be recognised as gemeinnuetzig (charitable) for education, ecology or culture; not suited to running a commercial farm as its main purpose, so communities pair an e.V. (membership, seminars, donations) with an eG or GmbH (land and business), as at Sieben Linden, Tempelhof and Hof Praedikow.

vehicles.name: Rechtsfaehige Stiftung (foundation) under sections 80 ff. BGB, incl. the Stiftung trias model
vehicles.note: Member-less legal person endowed to pursue a founder-set purpose permanently (section 80 BGB; Verbrauchsstiftung variant may spend down capital); state recognition required. The purpose-bound asset lock makes it the German analogue of a community land trust: Stiftung trias buys land and grants a long Erbbaurecht to the resident cooperative (Hof Praedikow since 2017), and Tempelhof runs a Stiftung am Tempelhof alongside its eG and e.V.

vehicles.name: Erbbaurecht (heritable building right) under the ErbbauRG
vehicles.note: A transferable, inheritable right to have a building on another's land (section 1 ErbbauRG), registered in the land register for typically 66 to 99 years; lets a Stiftung or Landgesellschaft keep the land off the market while residents or their eG own and finance the buildings; the de facto German CLT mechanism and the one used at Hof Praedikow and (as Erbpacht plots) at Eden Oranienburg since 1893.

vehicles.name: GmbH / gGmbH, including the Mietshaeuser Syndikat house-project model
vehicles.note: Limited company (EUR 25,000 capital, or UG with less) that can own land and run any business; a gGmbH is charitable (ZEGG operates as ZEGG gGmbH). The Mietshaeuser Syndikat (Freiburg, 1992; 191 projects, about 3,800 residents by June 2024) uses a Haus-GmbH owned 51 percent by the residents' Hausverein and 49 percent by the Syndikat GmbH, with each side holding a veto on sale, which permanently removes the property from the market; several rural projects (Hof Praedikow-type estates) use it.

vehicles.name: Trust
vehicles.note: Germany has no common-law trust; foreign trusts holding German land face transparency and inheritance-tax problems. Use a Stiftung or the Syndikat GmbH veto structure instead.

zoning.text: Foreigners buy freely; strict building code; farmland transfer regulated
zoning.build_on_farmland: Restrictive. Land outside a Bebauungsplan or the built-up village area is Aussenbereich under section 35 BauGB, where new buildings are permitted only for 'privileged' uses: a dwelling or barn that 'serves an agricultural or forestry business and occupies a subordinate part of its land' (section 35(1) no. 1), horticulture, renewable energy and similar; a residential eco-village is not privileged, and non-privileged projects are approved only case by case if they impair no public interests (section 35(2)), which planning offices routinely deny. Conversions of preserved farm buildings are allowed (section 35(4)) up to 5 additional dwellings per farmstead if the exterior is kept and abandonment was under 7 years. Practical routes: buy an existing Hofstelle or village plots inside the Innenbereich, convert barns, or persuade the municipality to adopt a Bebauungsplan for the project (the path taken by Sieben Linden and Tempelhof). Each Land's Bauordnung also requires building permits for anything but the smallest sheds; tiny houses and yurts as permanent dwellings need permits like any house.
zoning.communal_title: Communal ownership is straightforward: an eG, e.V., GmbH or Stiftung can be the registered owner, and co-ownership by individuals (Bruchteile) is possible but makes GrdstVG approval and financing harder. Transfers of agricultural land above state thresholds (0.15 to 2 ha) need GrdstVG approval; approval can be refused for an 'unhealthy distribution' when a non-farmer buys land a local farmer wants, for splitting agricultural parcels below 1 ha, or for a price grossly above market; the Landgesellschaft has a pre-emption right on parcels of 2 ha or more when approval would be refused (section 4 RSiedlG). Baden-Wuerttemberg applies its own ASVG. A community that is itself a registered farm business avoids most of these objections.
zoning.note: Section 35 BauGB is the single biggest practical obstacle for new rural communes in Germany: ownership of farmland does not bring any right to live on it. Budget 12 to 36 months for a municipal Bebauungsplan if a greenfield settlement is the goal, and expect building-code, fire-safety and wastewater standards comparable to any German new build.

climate.zone: Temperate oceanic (Koeppen Cfb) in the west and north grading to humid continental (Dfb) in the east and the Alpine foreland; annual precipitation about 515 mm (Berlin/Brandenburg) to 945 mm (Munich), 800 mm on the North Sea coast; summer daily highs 22 to 25 C, winters mild in the west and cold in the east; growing season roughly April to October.
climate.risks: Main hazards are river and flash floods (July 2021 Ahr/Erft floods: at least 184 dead in Germany, EUR 33.4 billion direct damage, the deadliest natural disaster since 1962) and increasingly frequent summer droughts and heat (2018: grain harvest down about 20 percent, rapeseed down 30 percent, farmers requested over EUR 1 billion in aid; the sandy soils of Brandenburg and the eastern lowlands are most drought-prone). Wildfire risk is rising in Brandenburg pine forests; the last German glacier is disappearing. ND-GAIN ranks Germany 3rd globally (score 69.2; vulnerability 0.301, readiness 0.682), so adaptive capacity is among the best anywhere.
climate.water: Generally water-rich with abundant groundwater and a dense river network; irrigation is rare except in Brandenburg and parts of Lower Saxony, where abstraction permits are now contested after the 2018-2022 dry years. Choose river-terrace or loess soils in the west and south for reliable rainfall, or expect to invest in rainwater retention and drought-tolerant rotations on the cheap sandy eastern land.

stabWhy.safe: Low homicide and violent crime; Numbeo safety index 60.87 (Oct 2026) reflects perception dips in big cities, rural areas remain very safe.

commune_history: Germany's communal-settlement tradition is long and legally entrenched: the Raiffeisen rural cooperatives of the 1860s led to the Genossenschaftsgesetz of 1889, the vegetarian Lebensreform colony Eden at Oranienburg was founded in 1893 by 18 Berliners as a cooperative holding 125 ha with Erbpacht garden plots and still exists today as Eden Gemeinnuetzige Obstbau-Siedlung eG with about 1,500 residents, and the Reichssiedlungsgesetz of 1919 created the non-profit Landgesellschaften whose pre-emption rights still shape farmland sales. After 1968 the Kommune movement produced income-sharing communes such as Kommune Niederkaufungen (1986) and the Kommuja network, the Mietshaeuser Syndikat (Freiburg, 1992) built a replicable anti-speculation GmbH model now spanning 191 projects, and post-reunification cheap eastern land enabled ZEGG (1991), Sieben Linden (1997), Schloss Tonndorf (2005) and Hof Praedikow (2017, Stiftung trias plus Erbbaurecht plus cooperative). A new group can point to these as fully recognised precedents, including municipalities that adopted dedicated development plans for ecovillages, and to the 2006 GenG amendment that expressly allows social and cultural cooperatives.
dealbreakers: Section 35 BauGB: owning farmland gives no right to live on it; new homes outside a village or Bebauungsplan are only allowed for a bona fide farm business, so a greenfield ecovillage needs a municipal development plan (12 to 36 months, political) or an existing farmstead to convert.

No passive-income, retiree, golden or nomad visa for non-EU members; each adult needs an individual permit (section 21 business, Blue Card/skilled worker, or discretionary section 7) and private health insurance that insurers can refuse to older or sick applicants.

Farmland costs EUR 35,300/ha on average (EUR 15,000 in the east) and sales to non-farmers can be refused under the Grundstueckverkehrsgesetz or pre-empted by the Landgesellschaft when a local farmer wants the parcel.

Worldwide taxation at up to 47.5 percent with full taxation of foreign pensions from 2025 and a planned 25 percent flat crypto tax from 2027, plus mandatory cooperative audits and German-language bureaucracy at every step.

name: Georgia
score_rationale: LAND 2: land is very cheap (USD 1,300-4,000/ha) but foreigners are barred from owning any agricultural land including homestead plots, so a foreign-majority group must lease or rely on a Georgian dominant partner. VISA 3: 365-day visa-free for 98 nationalities, business permits need only GEL 50,000 turnover, though PR is a 10-year road. TAX 3: territorial, 20% flat, 1% small-business, 0% on foreign pensions and crypto, no wealth tax. LAW 2: cooperative and NNLE forms exist and houses may be built on farmland, but co-op full membership is citizen-only and NGOs with foreign money face the 2024 foreign-influence law. LIFE 2: HDI 0.844, very safe, cheap, hospitable, but rural healthcare is weak and foreigners are outside state health cover. STAB 2: economy strong (7.5% growth 2025) and streets safe, but the 2024-26 political crisis, CPI/WJP/GPI all falling, and Russian occupation of 20% of territory keep it at 2.
verdict: The cheapest, easiest entry on Earth — 1-year visa-free, zero foreign-income tax — but you lease, don't own, and politics is turbulent.
summary: Georgia is the easiest place on this list to simply arrive and stay: citizens of 98 countries get 365 days visa-free (from 1 Jan 2026 you must carry health insurance of at least GEL 30,000), foreign-source income and foreign pensions are untaxed, and a one-person business pays 1% on turnover up to GEL 500,000. The catch for a commune is land: since the 2018 Constitution (Art. 19) and Organic Law 4848-IIს of 25 June 2019, agricultural land (including village 'homestead' plots) can only be owned by Georgian citizens or entities in which Georgian citizens hold more than 50%; a foreign-majority group must either put a trusted Georgian citizen as dominant partner, obtain a Government-approved investment plan, or lease. Expect cheap land (USD 1,300-4,000/ha in Kakheti), very safe villages, thin rural healthcare, a 10-year road to permanent residence, and an acute 2024-26 political crisis in which NGO-type vehicles with foreign funding are a political target.

land.ownership_note: Constitution of Georgia Art. 19(4) (in force Dec 2018) and the Organic Law on Agricultural Land Ownership No. 4848-IIს (adopted 25 June 2019) restrict ownership of agricultural land (pasture, hayfield, arable/perennial AND homestead categories) to the state, municipalities, Georgian citizens, and Georgian-registered legal entities or partnerships whose 'dominant partner' (>50% of shares or majority of members, with decisive influence, Art. 3(d)) is Georgian. Exceptions: (1) a foreign national who inherits must keep it in agricultural use (and historically alienate); (2) a Georgian company with a foreign dominant partner may own ag land only by decision of the Government of Georgia on the basis of an investment plan that develops an agricultural value chain and employs at least 4/5 Georgian citizens; failure triggers forced sale within 1 year (Art. 5(1)); (3) banks/IFIs temporarily after foreclosure. Art. 7 bars share transfers that would make a land-owning company foreign-dominated and Art. 6(2) bars pledging ag land to foreign-dominated creditors. A 100%-foreign LLC therefore cannot buy farmland. Workarounds actually used: a Georgian-citizen member (or NNLE whose members are majority Georgian) holds title with usufruct/lease contracts to the group (Ecovillage Georgia model); long-term lease from private owners or the state (the law regulates ownership only, leasing is unrestricted); or buying non-agricultural land, which foreigners may own without restriction, and converting ag land to non-agricultural purpose with a Government-set compensation fee (~GEL 34,000/ha cited for Tbilisi/Batumi, less elsewhere).

No statutory minimum parcel size for ag land; Soviet-era privatisation left typical household holdings of roughly 1 ha, so assembling 10-50 ha means buying from many owners.

visas.name: Short-term residence permit (property-based)
visas.requirement: Ownership of non-agricultural immovable property in Georgia with certified market value above USD 150,000 equivalent in GEL (raised from USD 100,000 effective 1 March 2026 following June 2025 amendments). Spouse and children included.
visas.initial_term: 1 year, renewable annually while property is held; no direct path to permanent residence
visas.processing_time: 30/20/10 calendar days for state fee GEL 300/450/600

visas.name: Investment residence permit
visas.requirement: Investment of at least USD 300,000 equivalent in GEL in a Georgian business or in non-agricultural real estate. Business route must show annual turnover of USD 50,000 in year 1, USD 100,000 in year 2 and USD 120,000 in years 3-5; real-estate route has no turnover test but property must be held 5 years. Spouse, minor children and dependents included.
visas.initial_term: Up to 5 years; after 5 years of maintained investment/property the holder may apply for an indefinite (permanent) residence permit

visas.name: Work residence permit (employment)
visas.requirement: Employment by a Georgian company with turnover of at least GEL 50,000 per foreign employee in the last 12 months (GEL 35,000 for schools/clinics); applicant's monthly income at least 5x the official subsistence minimum. Since the 2025-26 reform (phased 1 Sept 2025 to 1 March 2026, transition for existing labour migrants to 1 Jan 2027) the foreigner must first obtain the 'Right to Engage in Labour Activity'; a residence permit alone no longer authorises work; company directors count as workers. Penalties GEL 2,000 per violation.
visas.initial_term: 6-12 months first permit, then extensions; permanent residence after more than 10 years on temporary permits
visas.processing_time: 30/20/10 calendar days for GEL 300/450/600; apply at least 40 days before current stay expires

visas.name: Work residence permit via Individual Entrepreneur / own LLC (self-employed, farmer)
visas.requirement: Register as an Individual Entrepreneur (optionally with 1% Small Business Status) or found an LLC; the business must show GEL 50,000 turnover per foreigner over the prior 12 months and the applicant income of 5x subsistence minimum. From 2026 the labour-activity right must be obtained first. This is the realistic route for a commune farm business employing its own foreign members.
visas.initial_term: 6-12 months, renewable; up to 11 years cumulative on temporary permits before/while qualifying for permanent residence

visas.name: IT residence permit (new, 2026)
visas.requirement: IT professionals, IT entrepreneurs and executives with at least 2 years' IT experience and annual income of at least USD 25,000 in GEL equivalent. Revoked if absent from Georgia more than 183 consecutive days in a year. Georgia has no general digital-nomad visa; remote workers otherwise rely on the 365-day visa-free stay.
visas.initial_term: 3 years, renewable in 3-year increments up to 12 years

visas.name: Family reunification residence permit
visas.requirement: Spouse, minor children or dependent parents of a Georgian citizen or of a foreigner holding a residence permit; proof of relationship and sponsor's means.
visas.initial_term: Matches sponsor's permit; family of Georgian citizens may apply directly for permanent residence

visa_text: 1-year VISA-FREE for ~95 nationalities; residence via property/business; PR 5y
visa_detail: ~95 nationalities: 1 YEAR visa-free, NO application. Residence via property ($100k→$150k Mar 2026)/business. PR after 5 yr of permits · citizenship ~10 yr.
visa_note: There is no retiree, rentista or passive-income permit; pensioners use the 365-day visa-free stay (insurance now mandatory) or the USD 150,000 property permit. Permanent residence requires more than 10 years of continuous temporary permits (or 5 years on the USD 300,000 investment route, or marriage to a citizen); naturalisation requires 10 consecutive years of lawful residence plus Georgian language, history and law tests and a demonstrated connection (property, business, employment). Dual citizenship is possible only by exception. Flag: the 2025-26 reform replaced labour-migrant registration with a mandatory work-authorisation step and raised the property threshold to USD 150,000 on 1 March 2026.

tax.text: Territorial — foreign income untaxed; 1% small-business; 5% dividends
tax.capital_gains: Georgian-source gains taxed at 20% PIT except sale of a house/apartment with attached land and vehicles at 5% (Tax Code; residential property held over 2 years is exempt in practice); residential rental income 5% without deductions. Gains on cryptocurrency sales by individuals are exempt under Ministry of Finance Public Decision No. 201 of 28 June 2019 (crypto deemed not Georgian-source) and crypto-to-fiat sales are VAT-exempt.
tax.wealth_tax: None. No inheritance or gift tax between first- and second-degree relatives.
tax.property_tax: Property tax on buildings only for households whose annual family income exceeds GEL 40,000 (0.05-1% of market value, set by municipality); separate annual land tax on agricultural land set by municipality within statutory base rates, due 15 November. No stamp duty; registration at the Public Registry costs about GEL 50-200.
tax.foreign_pension: Not taxed: resident individuals are exempt on income without a Georgian source, which covers foreign state and private pensions, foreign rental income and foreign investment income.
tax.special_regime: Small Business Status: individual entrepreneurs with turnover up to GEL 500,000 pay 1% of turnover (3% above the cap); Micro Business under GEL 30,000 with no employees is fully exempt. Dividends and interest 5% withholding, final. Corporate profit tax 15% only on distributed profits (Estonian model). VAT 18% with registration threshold GEL 100,000. Mandatory pension contributions 2% employee + 2% employer (4% for self-employed), not applied to those over 60.
tax.crypto: Individuals: 0% on crypto capital gains and no VAT (MoF Public Decision No. 201/29062 of 2019); mining and company-run trading are taxed normally.
tax.coop_treatment: Agricultural cooperatives with status under Law 816-RS (2013) are eligible for state grants, preferential credit and tax privileges defined in the Tax Code; a cooperative is a commercial entity under the Law on Entrepreneurs and otherwise follows the 15% distributed-profit regime.

cost.note: Country-level frugal budget is ~USD 574/month (globalcostdata 2026); Tbilisi budget living USD 600-900. In a Kakheti or Imereti village with a USD 150-250 rented room/house, USD 150-200 groceries, USD 40-80 utilities/wood, USD 20 phone/internet and USD 20 private health insurance, USD 500-700 per adult is realistic; with owned housing and a garden, USD 400-500. Georgians outside Tbilisi live on well under USD 600.

health.system: State Universal Healthcare Programme (UHCP, since 2013) funds a basic package for citizens, increasingly income-targeted, through mostly private hospitals; large private insurers (GPI, Imedi L, Ardi, TBC, Aldagi, Unison) cover the rest. Rural care is thin: district clinics handle primary care, anything serious means Telavi/Kutaisi/Batumi or Tbilisi.
health.cost_for_residents: Basic local private plan USD 15-25/month (GEL 500-700/year); broader plans USD 50-100/month. Out-of-pocket: GP visit USD 10-25, specialist USD 20-50, hospital night USD 50-200, ER USD 30-80.
health.immigrant_access: Residence-permit holders are NOT automatically covered by UHCP; only those registered as socially vulnerable (low-income) qualify, so in practice foreigners buy private insurance, which is sold without a residence permit. Since 1 January 2026 visa-free entrants must hold health and accident insurance with at least GEL 30,000 cover; residence-permit holders are exempt from that entry requirement.
health.quality_note: Numbeo health-care index 56.3 (moderate). Tbilisi private hospitals are adequate; quality drops noticeably outside the capital and most expats travel to Tbilisi for anything beyond basic care.

pension.text: Foreign pensions untaxed; no retiree visa needed (visa-free)
pension.foreign_pension_tax: 0% - foreign pensions are foreign-source income and exempt for resident individuals under Georgia's territorial system; no reporting of foreign assets.
pension.retiree_visa: None. Retirees stay 365 days visa-free (insurance mandatory from 2026) or buy non-agricultural property above USD 150,000 for a renewable 1-year permit; USD 300,000 property gives a 5-year permit convertible to indefinite residence.

ag.subsidies: Rural Development Agency (RDA, NNLE under the Ministry of Environmental Protection and Agriculture) runs 'Plant the Future' (co-finances up to 80% of saplings and 60% of drip irrigation for orchards; ~8,546 ha planted 2015-19, GEL 50.5m state co-financing), preferential agro-credit, agro-insurance and commodity subsidies (grape purchase subsidy, hazelnut inputs GEL 22.6m in 2024). Subsidies were 54% of agricultural spending in 2024 and function 'more as social assistance' (FREE Network, Mar 2025). Beneficiaries must be registered Georgian farms or cooperatives; a foreign-owned LLC that cannot own ag land is effectively outside most schemes.
ag.coop_law: Law of Georgia on Agricultural Cooperatives No. 816-RS of 12 July 2013: a cooperative formed under the Law on Entrepreneurs with at least 5 members (3 in high-mountain settlements) can obtain 'agricultural cooperative status' from the Agency, giving access to state grants, preferential credit and tax privileges. Full shareholder-members must be Georgian citizens aged 18+ engaged in agriculture; foreign nationals and foreign legal entities may only be associate members.
ag.equipment_note: RDA and donor (EU ENPARD, FAO, USAID until 2025 cuts) programmes have co-financed machinery, cold storage and processing for cooperatives; EU and US budget support to the government was suspended after November 2024, so donor-funded rural programmes are shrinking.

legal.text: Kooperativi, association, foundation; land co-op mechanism exists

vehicles.name: Agricultural cooperative (kooperativi) with status under Law 816-RS (2013)
vehicles.note: Best fit for the farm business and for subsidies, but full members must be Georgian citizens and the co-op can only own ag land if Georgians are the dominant members; foreigners join as associate members.

vehicles.name: Non-entrepreneurial (non-commercial) legal entity - NNLE association (a(a)ip) under the Civil Code
vehicles.note: The vehicle Ecovillage Georgia uses: the NNLE holds title and grants members usufruct; it can own ag land only if Georgian citizens are the majority of members (Organic Law 4848 Art. 4). Foreign funding above 20% now triggers 'foreign-influence' registration under the 2024 law, a live political risk.

vehicles.name: NNLE foundation (pondi)
vehicles.note: Asset-holding form without members; same Georgian-dominance test for ag land applies through its founders/board, and the same foreign-agent exposure.

vehicles.name: Limited liability company (shps) under the Law on Entrepreneurs (2021)
vehicles.note: Cheapest to run (1-day registration, 15% tax only on distributions); can own ag land if a Georgian citizen holds >50% and decisive control, or with a Government-approved investment plan employing 4/5 Georgians. Share transfers that would make it foreign-dominated are void (Art. 7).

vehicles.name: Long-term lease / usufruct of agricultural land
vehicles.note: The Organic Law regulates ownership only, so foreigners and foreign-owned entities may lease private or state ag land for long terms and register the lease at the Public Registry; the standard workaround.

vehicles.name: Community land trust (no statutory form)
vehicles.note: Not recognised; emulate with an NNLE owning land plus registered usufruct/lease contracts to residents, as Ecovillage Georgia does. Common-law trusts are not recognised in Georgian civil law.

zoning.text: Foreigners BARRED from agricultural land (2017 moratorium); company workaround; non-ag OK
zoning.build_on_farmland: Permitted in principle: Law 4849-IIს of 25 June 2019 allows individual residential houses, agricultural buildings and ancillary buildings on agricultural land without changing its category, subject to a municipal construction permit; any other use needs a change of designated purpose decided by the National Agency of Public Registry with a Government-set compensation fee (practitioners cite ~GEL 34,000/ha in Tbilisi/Batumi, far less in villages). Village houses sit on 'homestead' plots, which are themselves an agricultural category.
zoning.communal_title: No communal or collective title category outside Soviet-era pasture commons; multiple households can co-own as a partnership only if Georgian citizens are the majority. Foreigners' practical route is NNLE/LLC title with Georgian dominance plus usufruct, or lease.
zoning.note: Fragmentation is the practical constraint: 1992-98 privatisation produced ~1 ha household parcels, so a 20 ha site means consolidating many titles with sometimes unregistered boundaries; budget for surveying and Public Registry 'systematic registration'.

climate.zone: Three belts: humid subtropical west (Adjara, Guria, Samegrelo, Imereti; 1,500-2,500 mm rain, citrus, hazelnut, tea), dry continental east (Kakheti, Kvemo Kartli; 400-700 mm, vineyards and grain needing irrigation), and alpine highlands (Svaneti, Racha, Javakheti; short seasons, pasture). Numbeo climate index 88.5.
climate.risks: Floods, landslides, mudflows and avalanches along 20,000+ rivers and steep terrain; roughly 40% of the population lives in hazard-prone areas. Eastern Georgia faces drought (19% of population drought-exposed), hail and soil degradation; western Georgia faces landslides and floods (Guria, September 2023). Earthquake zone (Racha 1991 M7.0). ND-GAIN 55.3 (rank 48; vulnerability 0.413, readiness 0.519).
climate.water: Abundant in the west; the east depends on Soviet-era irrigation networks (Alazani, Mtkvari basins) that the state is rehabilitating. Verify a working irrigation right before buying in Kakheti or Kvemo Kartli.

life_text: Cheap, hospitable; rural healthcare poor
stab_text: Political crisis 2024–26, EU path frozen, protests

stabWhy.pol: 2024-26 political crisis: disputed Oct 2024 election, EU accession halted 28 Nov 2024 until at least 2028, 'foreign influence' law targeting NGOs, EU/US funding cuts and sanctions on officials, continuous protests.
stabWhy.law: WJP 2025 score 0.58 (rank 52, down 2.4%); CPI 2025 fell to 50 (lowest since 2013) with TI citing state capture and politically motivated prosecutions.
stabWhy.safe: Numbeo safety index 73.5 (high); petty crime and bribery rare; villages are very safe.
stabWhy.econ: GDP +7.5% in 2025, inflation ~4%, policy rate 8%, lari stable near 2.7/USD; but FDI-dependent, remittance- and Russia-exposed, and Western support withdrawn.
stabWhy.peace: GPI 2025 rank 109 of 163 (score 2.185), down two years running; Russia occupies Abkhazia and South Ossetia (~20% of territory) with a frozen conflict line.
stabWhy.clim: ND-GAIN 55.3 (rank 48) but 40% of the population in flood/landslide/drought-prone areas and weak rural disaster governance.

commune_history: Georgia's oldest living communal precedent is the Doukhobors, Russian pacifist sectarians exiled to the Javakheti plateau in 1841-45 who built eight villages around Gorelovka with a common economy, orphanage and school and later ran what doukhobor.org calls 'the last collective farm'; a few hundred remain. Soviet collectivisation (kolkhoz/sovkhoz, 1929-91) was reversed by the 1992-98 privatisation that handed ~1 ha household plots to rural families, which is why Georgian farmland is fragmented and why the Law on Agricultural Cooperatives (No. 816-RS, 2013) exists to re-aggregate it. Since the 2018 Constitution and 2019 Organic Law closed farmland ownership to foreigners, the live precedent for a mixed Georgian-international group is Ecovillage Georgia (Lagodekhi, land bought 2023 under an NGO with resident usufruct rights) and the 1989 TEMI social-therapy community in Gremi, which farms and makes wine as a Georgian NGO.
dealbreakers: No freehold farmland for foreigners: Organic Law 4848-IIს (2019) bars foreign nationals and foreign-dominated entities from owning agricultural land, including village homestead plots; your title must sit with a Georgian citizen-majority entity or be a lease.

The 2024 'foreign influence' law and the 2024-26 crackdown on NGOs: a commune organised as an NNLE funded by foreign members is exactly the profile the government labels an 'organisation serving a foreign power'.

Permanent residence takes more than 10 years of continuous temporary permits (unless USD 300,000 is invested); 365-day visa-free stays never accrue, and from 2026 every working member needs separate labour authorisation.
Rural healthcare and emergency response are thin and foreigners are outside the state health programme; serious cases mean a trip to Tbilisi.
languages: Georgian (official); Russian widely understood by over-40s; English in Tbilisi and among younger people; Armenian and Azerbaijani in minority regions (Javakheti, Kvemo Kartli).
currency: Georgian lari (GEL); roughly 2.67 GEL per USD in 2025-26 (XE 12-month average 0.3745 USD/GEL).

verification.overall: The record is substantially accurate. Primary sources (matsne.gov.ge) confirm the agricultural-land regime, the residence-permit tiers (USD 150k property, USD 300k investment with the stated turnover ladder, 10-year PR rule), and PwC confirms the tax figures; GPI, CPI, ND-GAIN and HDI values match. One correction is needed: the labour-permit reform timeline is Government Ordinance No. 70 of 20 Feb 2026 launching 1 March 2026 (self-employed enforcement 1 May 2026, employees by 1 Jan 2027), with escalating fines GEL 2,000/4,000/12,000, not a 1 Sept 2025 phase-in with a flat GEL 2,000 fine. Not found: GEL 35,000 school/clinic threshold, 5x subsistence-minimum rule, GEL 500-1,000 overstay fines. tbilisi-expat.com states PR after 6 years for non-investors, but the statute text says 10, so the record's 10y stands.

name: Uruguay
score_rationale: LAND 2: fully ownable by foreigners with a clean registry, but no longer cheap (record USD 4,178/ha average in 2025, USD 7,000-10,000 in the prime south-west). VISA 3: direct permanent residency on ~USD 1,500/month per person, work allowed, citizenship in 3-5 years; only the 12-24-month processing time and 183-day presence rule weigh against it. TAX 2: territorial system leaves foreign pensions and (for 11 years) foreign capital income untaxed, but local farm income faces 36% top IRPF / 25% IRAE, 22% VAT, high social charges and a 0.1% wealth tax, and Ley 20.446 tightened the holiday from 2026. LAW 2: world-class cooperative statute (18.407), FUCVAM collective-ownership precedent, trusts and foundations, but rural land cannot be subdivided for housing (5 ha minimum) and departmental permits govern every dwelling. LIFE 3: HDI 0.862, universal SNIS health, Numbeo QoL 143. STAB 3: strongest rule of law and lowest fragility in Latin America; only climate volatility and moderate urban crime detract.
verdict: The region's stable, high-QoL bet: own farmland freely, an 11-year foreign-income holiday, and famous housing co-ops.
summary: Uruguay lets foreigners buy farmland outright with the same rights as locals (hold it personally, or through a company whose shares are nominative and owned by natural persons, per Ley 18.092), grants permanent residency directly to anyone showing roughly USD 1,500/month of income, and taxes only Uruguayan-source income: foreign pensions are untaxed and foreign dividends/interest are tax-free for 11 years if you spend more than 183 days a year in the country (Ley 20.446 rules from 1 Jan 2026). Farmland averaged a record USD 4,178/ha in 2025 (USD 2,300 in Artigas to USD 9,707 in Colonia) and rural parcels cannot be subdivided below 5 ha or turned into housing lots, so a commune should buy one parcel through a cooperativa (Ley 18.407), asociación civil (Ley 17.163) or fideicomiso (Ley 17.703) and build member housing under a departmental building permit. Budget 12-24 months for residency paperwork, about USD 1,300/month per adult in a small town, and serious water storage: the 2022-23 drought cost about 3% of GDP and was followed by 2024 floods.

land.text: Cheap grazing/farmland by global standards; foreigners own FREELY
land.ownership_note: No nationality, residency, reciprocity, size-cap or border-zone restriction: a foreign natural person buys rural land freehold on identical terms to a Uruguayan. The only structural rule is Ley 18.092 (7 Jan 2007): rural land and farm operations may be owned by individuals, or by companies (SA, SAS, SRL, etc.) only if the entire capital is nominative shares/quotas held by natural persons; an SA with bearer shares or with a corporate/foreign-company shareholder needs case-by-case authorisation from the Executive (MGAP + MEF), which has been granted to about 90 companies holding ~6 million ha. Co-ops, asociaciones civiles and fideicomisos can hold rural land. Ley 11.029 art. 35 gives the Instituto Nacional de Colonización a right of first refusal on any sale of 500 ha CONEAT-100-equivalent or more. Prices are set and paid in USD; DIEA (MGAP) publishes the official price series: 2025 average USD 4,178/ha (+5% on 2024's USD 3,967, a 25-year record) over 1,718 sales and 259,000 ha; departmental averages ran from USD 2,300 (Artigas, northern grazing) to USD 6,842 (San José), USD 7,964 (Soriano) and USD 9,707 (Colonia, prime cropland/dairy). Expect USD 2,000-3,500/ha for rough grazing in Artigas/Salto/Tacuarembó/Cerro Largo and USD 6,000-12,000/ha for prime litoral cropland.
land.build_rules: Ley 18.308 (Ordenamiento Territorial, 2008): subdividing rural land into lots under 5 ha is prohibited (3 ha in Montevideo, Canelones, San José, Maldonado and Colonia); rural land is excluded by definition from urbanisation and residential fraccionamiento, with exceptions down to 1 ha only where a departmental land-use instrument designates them and for MEVIR programmes. Rural subdivisions need DGRN (Dirección General de Registros / Catastro) and departmental approval. Farm dwellings and agricultural buildings on a single rural padrón are allowed with a departmental (Intendencia) building permit.
land.cheap_house_program: None for foreigners. MEVIR (state rural-housing agency) builds subsidised houses for low-income rural workers only; Uruguay has no EUR-1-house style scheme.
land.note: Transaction costs: notary (escribano) ~3% + ITP transfer tax 2% buyer and 2% seller + registry fees; title searches are reliable (public registry, no title insurance culture). Cadastral values used for taxes are far below market.

visas.name: Residencia legal permanente por medios de vida propios (rentista / independent means)
visas.requirement: No statutory minimum; Dirección Nacional de Migración applies a solvency test. Practitioners cite ~USD 1,500/month per single applicant, ~USD 2,500-3,000/month per couple or family, from passive or remote foreign sources (rent, dividends, interest, annuities, remote salary). Documents: apostilled birth certificate, police clearance from countries of residence, proof of income, medical certificate issued in Uruguay, local address.
visas.initial_term: Permanent residency granted directly (no temporary phase); an interim 'hoja de identidad provisoria' and provisional cédula are issued on filing and allow living, renting and buying property.
visas.processing_time: 12-24 months from complete filing (2025-26 practice); the citizenship clock starts on the filing date, not approval.

Note this grants LEGAL residency only; the TAX-residency holiday now needs UI 12.5 million (~USD 2 million) of real estate, USD 100,000/yr into the innovation fund, or >183 days/yr presence (Ley 20.446, from 1 Jan 2026).

visa_text: Straightforward residency via income; clear path to citizenship
visa_detail: Residence via steady income (~$1,500/mo); clear path. 6–12 mo. Citizenship 3 yr (married) / 5 yr — famously accessible.
visa_note: All main routes lead straight to permanent legal residency; naturalisation ('ciudadanía legal') takes 3 years of residence for married applicants or those with family in Uruguay and 5 years for singles, counted from the filing date, with a 183-day-per-year presence rule (absences over 6 consecutive months reset the clock), a Spanish-language interview at the Corte Electoral, and dual citizenship allowed. Caveat: legal citizens are issued passports that record the country of birth rather than Uruguayan nationality, which has caused visa-free travel problems. Legal residency and tax residency are separate statuses with separate tests.

tax.text: Territorial; ~11-year tax holiday on foreign income; low property
tax.capital_gains: 12% flat IRPF on Uruguayan-source capital gains and capital income (rents, interest, dividends, sale of property); real-estate gains may be computed on the actual gain or a notional 15% of the sale price. Foreign-source capital income: exempt during the holiday, then 12% (or the 7% option).
tax.wealth_tax: Impuesto al Patrimonio: 0.1% flat for resident individuals on net assets above about USD 160,000 (2026; doubled for a family unit); non-residents outside IRNR 0.7-1.5%. Rural real estate actually used in agricultural production can be exempt for individuals under the agricultural-assets rules (verify thresholds with a contador).
tax.property_tax: Contribución Inmobiliaria Rural is departmental, roughly 0.5-1.5% of cadastral value (Montevideo rural ~0.525%), computed on land value with a 20% deduction and a further 10% discount for owners who personally run the farm; cadastral values are far below market, so a USD 500,000 farm typically pays a few hundred USD a year. VAT 22%.
tax.foreign_pension: Not taxed. IRPF reaches foreign-source income only for passive capital returns (interest, dividends) and for employment services rendered abroad to Uruguayan taxpayers; a foreign state or private pension is foreign-source income outside the IRPF net regardless of the tax holiday.
tax.special_regime: Tax holiday for new tax residents on foreign-source capital income (interest, dividends, foreign rents): exempt for the year of arrival plus 10 years (11 years total), or alternatively a flat 7% rate indefinitely instead of 12%. Ley 20.446 (Budget Law 2025-2029, enacted 16 Dec 2025) applies to anyone becoming tax resident from 1 Jan 2026: the option is exercised once and requires either (a) more than 183 days of presence in Uruguay each year, (b) real estate above UI 12,500,000 (~USD 2 million), or (c) UI 625,000 (~USD 100,000) per year into certified innovation/venture funds; the old UI 3.5 million (~USD 560,000) property + 60-day route is abolished for new entrants. After the holiday, a further 5 years at a halved 6% rate is available with UI 6.25 million in property or UI 625,000/yr in funds, or a fixed annual payment of UI 1.875 million (~USD 300,000) for 20 years. Earlier residents keep their original terms.
tax.crypto: No crypto-specific tax statute. DGI Consulta 6.419 (2021) treats crypto as intangible movable property: an occasional sale by an individual is a 12% IRPF Category I capital gain if Uruguayan-source; trades on foreign exchanges from foreign accounts are generally foreign-source and untaxed for resident individuals. Ley 20.345 (2024) regulates virtual-asset service providers under the BCU.
tax.coop_treatment: Cooperatives under Ley 18.407 enjoy national tax exemptions (historically IRAE income-tax and Impuesto al Patrimonio exemptions for agrarian, worker and housing co-ops carried into the 2008 law) and pay a 0.15% 'prestación coactiva' on turnover to INACOOP; confirm the current exemption list with INACOOP before relying on it.

cost.note: Interior town / rural budget per adult excluding land: rent USD 400-600 for a small house in an inland town (USD 0 if housed on the farm), groceries USD 350-500, utilities USD 100-250 (electricity is expensive; UTE tariffs are among the region's highest), health USD 50-150 (mutualista or ASSE), transport/fuel USD 100-150. Practitioners put a modest interior lifestyle at USD 1,200-1,600 and a bare minimum at USD 1,000-1,200; Montevideo and Punta del Este run USD 2,000+. Numbeo cost-of-living index 52.9 (Sep 2026).

health.system: Sistema Nacional Integrado de Salud (SNIS, 2007-08 reform) funded through FONASA: workers and pensioners pay 3-8% of income into FONASA and choose a provider; public provider ASSE (hospitals and rural polyclinics) plus ~40 non-profit 'mutualistas' and private insurers. Rural areas rely on ASSE polyclinics with referral to departmental hospitals; Montevideo has the tertiary care.
health.cost_for_residents: ASSE free or ~USD 40-80/month; mutualista USD 50-150/month private-pay or FONASA-covered with co-pays (tickets/órdenes of a few USD).
health.immigrant_access: Legal residents (and applicants with the provisional ID) can join ASSE directly, free of charge if household income is under 62 UR plus 2.5 UR per family member, otherwise about USD 40-80/month; anyone employed or registered as a contributor is enrolled in FONASA and may choose a mutualista with no monthly fee beyond co-pays. Without FONASA, direct mutualista membership costs roughly USD 50-150/month depending on age and plan. Mercosur residents have a simplified enrolment path.
health.quality_note: Numbeo health-care index 68.8 (high); life expectancy ~78; universal coverage and strong primary care, but waiting times for specialists in the interior and limited rural emergency capacity.

pension.text: Residency via pension; foreign income holiday
pension.foreign_pension_tax: 0%: foreign pensions are foreign-source income outside the territorial IRPF. Only foreign passive capital income (interest, dividends, foreign rents) is ever reached, and that is exempt for 11 years under the new-resident holiday (or taxed at the 7% option / 12% standard).
pension.retiree_visa: Pensionado route: documented foreign pension of roughly USD 1,500/month per person (no statutory floor) gives permanent legal residency directly, work allowed, citizenship after 3 (married) or 5 (single) years; processing 12-24 months.

ag.subsidies: Uruguay is a low-subsidy, export-oriented farm economy with no EU-style area payments. Support is targeted: MGAP's Dirección General de Desarrollo Rural (DGDR) runs non-reimbursable grant calls for registered 'productores familiares' (e.g. 2025-26 water-infrastructure subsidies for 500 family dairy/cattle farms financed by the World Bank with INAC; 'Más valor a la producción familiar' value-chain grants; rural-youth programmes), the Fondo Agropecuario de Emergencia pays drought/flood relief, and the Instituto Plan Agropecuario provides free extension. Family-producer registration requires a small holding (up to 500 ha CONEAT-100), at most 2 permanent hired workers and residence on or near the farm, so a cooperative of resident smallholders can qualify.
ag.coop_law: Ley 18.407 (24 Oct 2008, Ley General de Cooperativas): single statute for all co-op classes including cooperativas agrarias, de trabajo, de vivienda, de consumo and sociales; minimum members vary by class (agrarian co-ops are formed by producers); registration with the Registro de Personas Jurídicas; INACOOP (created by art. 186) promotes and partly finances co-ops. Housing co-ops with collective ownership and user rights are governed by Ley 13.728 (17 Dec 1968) and federated in FUCVAM (600+ co-ops, ~18,000 inhabited homes). Agrarian co-ops are federated in Cooperativas Agrarias Federadas (CAF).
ag.equipment_note: No special duty-free equipment regime for newcomers; agricultural machinery imports pay Mercosur common external tariff rates unless the farm qualifies under the Ley 16.906 investment-promotion scheme (COMAP), which can exempt IRAE and import duties for approved projects.

legal.text: Cooperativa (very strong — housing co-ops famous), asociación, fundación

vehicles.name: Cooperativa agraria (Ley 18.407, 2008)
vehicles.note: Best fit for the farm business: producer-members pool land use, machinery and marketing; can own rural land outright (Ley 18.092 does not restrict co-ops); national tax exemptions and INACOOP/CAF support; one-member-one-vote governance by statute.

vehicles.name: Cooperativa de vivienda de usuarios por ayuda mutua (Ley 13.728, 1968 + Ley 18.407)
vehicles.note: The FUCVAM model: the co-op owns the land and houses collectively, members hold use-and-enjoyment rights and are refunded their labour/savings on leaving, so homes cannot be sold on the market. Designed for urban/suburban housing with state loans, but it is the live precedent for collective-tenure housing in Uruguay and can be combined with an agrarian co-op on rural land.

vehicles.name: Cooperativa de trabajo (worker co-op, Ley 18.407)
vehicles.note: For members who are workers rather than landholding producers (processing, agro-tourism, education); members are registered with BPS as self-employed co-operators.

vehicles.name: Asociación civil (Civil Code art. 21; Ley 17.163, 1999; MEC registry)
vehicles.note: Non-profit membership body with legal personality via the Ministerio de Educación y Cultura; can own rural land and run educational/cultural programmes; surplus cannot be distributed; good for the community/values layer rather than the farm P&L.

vehicles.name: Fundación (Ley 17.163, 1999)
vehicles.note: Asset-holding non-profit with a founder-endowed patrimony and purpose; a workable stand-in for a community land trust that holds the land permanently off the market while a co-op or members farm it under lease.

vehicles.name: Fideicomiso (Ley 17.703, 27 Oct 2003)
vehicles.note: Uruguayan trust: settlor transfers land to a trustee (fiduciario, registered with the BCU for financial trusts) for named beneficiaries under written instructions; widely used for land and agribusiness (fideicomisos agropecuarios); lets a group separate land title from members' personal estates and inheritance.

vehicles.name: Sociedad por Acciones Simplificada (SAS, Ley 19.820, 2019) or SRL/SA with nominative shares
vehicles.note: Ordinary companies may own rural land only if all capital is nominative shares held by natural persons (Ley 18.092); otherwise MGAP/MEF authorisation is needed. Simple and fast, but carries IRAE corporate tax and makes the land a saleable asset.

vehicles.name: Colonia del Instituto Nacional de Colonización (Ley 11.029, 1948)
vehicles.note: State colonisation body administering ~600,000 ha (400,000 ha leased, 200,000 ha under purchase promise) for 5,000+ families; parcels are allocated by call with legal preference for cooperative groups, and colonists must live on and work the land (relaxed by the 2020 LUC). Low rents, but allocation favours Uruguayan family producers and foreigners should treat it as a long shot.

vehicles.name: Community land trust
vehicles.note: No CLT statute; replicate with a fundación or fideicomiso holding title and granting long leases or user rights to a cooperativa.

zoning.text: Foreigners own land freely incl. farmland — no restrictions
zoning.build_on_farmland: Permitted for farm dwellings and agricultural buildings with an Intendencia building permit, but Ley 18.308 (2008) bars residential subdivision of rural land and sets a 5 ha minimum lot (3 ha in Montevideo, Canelones, San José, Maldonado and Colonia; 1 ha only where a departmental plan designates it). Several houses for members/workers on one rural padrón are normally approvable as 'vivienda rural' tied to the farm, but each department applies its own ordinance (Maldonado and Rocha protect 'suelo rural natural' on the coast and sierras) and selling individual house lots is not possible without a formal change of land category.
zoning.communal_title: Title is held by one entity (cooperativa, asociación civil, fundación, fideicomiso or company) or in condominio (co-ownership shares); the FUCVAM collective-ownership/user-rights model under Ley 13.728 is the recognised legal template for members holding use rights without individual titles.
zoning.note: Check the departmental 'directrices' and local plans (Ley 18.308 instruments) before buying: some coastal and sierra zones restrict new construction, and off-grid water/sanitation need Intendencia approval. Rural electricity (UTE) and internet (Antel fibre/4G) reach most of the country.

climate.zone: Humid subtropical (Köppen Cfa) across the whole country: mild winters (occasional frost, no snow), hot humid summers, rain in all seasons averaging roughly 1,000 mm in the south to 1,400 mm in the north-east; Numbeo climate index 98 (very high). Year-round pasture growth; good for cattle, dairy, rice, soy, wheat, citrus, vines and horticulture.
climate.risks: High inter-annual rainfall variability tied to ENSO: the 2022-23 drought was the worst in 74 years, hit over 60% of the territory, caused ~USD 1.8 billion of farm losses (~3% of GDP) and the 2023 Montevideo drinking-water crisis; it was followed by March-May 2024 floods that triggered an agricultural emergency and displaced 2,800+ people, and a renewed drought alert in February 2025. No hurricanes, earthquakes or volcanoes; occasional severe storms, hail and tornadoes. ND-GAIN 56.6 (rank 52): low vulnerability, high readiness.
climate.water: Abundant surface water (Río Negro, Uruguay, Santa Lucía basins) and the Guaraní aquifer in the north-west, but on-farm supply depends on rain-fed dams (tajamares) and wells; the state (OSE) supplies towns. After 2023 the MGAP subsidises water reservoirs and pumping for family farms; a commune should budget for a dam, deep well and rainwater storage.

life_text: Safest, most stable in region; temperate
stab_text: 'Switzerland of South America' — top rule of law

stabWhy.pol: Most stable democracy in Latin America: Fragile States Index 33.7 (lowest in the region), routine peaceful alternation of power, CPI 73 (#17 worldwide).
stabWhy.law: WJP Rule of Law 0.72 (#23 of 143, first in Latin America) and CPI 73; reliable property registry and courts, though slow.
stabWhy.safe: Numbeo safety index 47.3 (moderate): property crime and drug-related homicide concentrated in Montevideo's periphery; rural interior is quiet. GPI 'societal safety' is the country's weakest peace domain.
stabWhy.econ: Investment-grade sovereign, floating peso with inflation inside the 3-6% target band, USD-denominated land market; exposure to commodity cycles and a high cost structure.
stabWhy.peace: GPI 2025 rank 48 (1.784), improving to 43 in the 2026 edition; no internal or external conflict, non-aligned foreign policy.
stabWhy.clim: ND-GAIN 56.6 (rank 52) with low vulnerability, but the 2022-23 drought cost ~3% of GDP and 2024 floods followed; water security is the live risk.

commune_history: Uruguay was settled in part by group colonies that still exist: Waldensian Italians founded Colonia Valdense in 1858, Swiss settlers Nueva Helvecia in 1862, and three waves of Prussian Mennonites founded El Ombú (1950, 1,200 ha for ~80 families), Gartental (1951) and Colonia Delta (1955), each run through its own producer-consumer cooperative. The state institutionalised group land settlement with the Instituto Nacional de Colonización (Ley 11.029, 1948), which today administers about 600,000 ha for 5,000+ families and gives statutory preference to applicants organised as cooperatives, and with the National Housing Law 13.728 (1968) that created the FUCVAM mutual-aid housing cooperatives (600+ co-ops, ~18,000 homes) holding land and houses in collective ownership with member user rights. Comunidad del Sur, an anarchist commune founded in Montevideo in 1955 and re-established after exile on a 13-ha organic farm at Camino Maldonado km 16, is the country's longest-running secular intentional community. The General Cooperative Law 18.407 (2008) and INACOOP give any new group a clear, tested legal path.
dealbreakers: Land is not cheap: 2025 average USD 4,178/ha and USD 7,000-10,000/ha in the productive south-west, so a 50-ha farm with water and a house runs USD 250,000-600,000, paid in USD.

Rural land cannot be subdivided into house lots (5 ha minimum, residential fraccionamiento banned under Ley 18.308): members cannot get individual titled homesteads, and every dwelling needs a departmental permit.
Residency takes 12-24 months and citizenship/tax-holiday rules require >183 days of physical presence per year; absences over 6 months reset the citizenship clock.
Rain-fed farming with ENSO whiplash: the 2022-23 drought (worst in 74 years, ~3% of GDP in losses) and 2024 floods show a commune without its own reservoirs and wells can lose two seasons.
languages: Spanish (official); Portuñol in the Brazilian border departments; English limited outside Montevideo and Punta del Este.
currency: Uruguayan peso (UYU); rural land and housing are priced and transacted in USD.

corrections.old: Territorial; ~11-year tax holiday on foreign income; low property
corrections.new: The holiday covers only foreign-source CAPITAL income (interest, dividends, foreign rents), not all foreign income (foreign pensions/salaries are simply out of scope). From 1 Jan 2026 (Ley 20.446, Budget 2025-2029) new residents must spend >183 days/yr in Uruguay or invest UI 12.5M (~USD 2M) in property or USD 100k/yr in innovation funds to use it; the USD 560k property + 60-day route is abolished.

corrections.old: Foreigners own land freely incl. farmland — no restrictions
corrections.new: True for natural persons, but Ley 18.092 (2007) allows companies to hold rural land only if all shares are nominative and owned by natural persons (otherwise MGAP/MEF authorisation), and Ley 11.029 art. 35 gives the INC first refusal on sales of 500+ ha CONEAT-100. Ley 18.308 bars residential subdivision of rural land (5 ha minimum lots).
Processing is 12-24 months from complete filing in 2025-26 practice (an interim provisional ID is issued on filing and the citizenship clock starts then).

corrections.old: Residency via pension; foreign income holiday
corrections.new: Foreign pensions are not covered by the holiday; they are foreign-source labour income outside the territorial IRPF altogether, so untaxed indefinitely.

verification.overall: Record is largely accurate: land-market figures, land-ownership law, INC right of first refusal, residency benchmarks and timelines, index values, ASSE thresholds, communities and the drought dealbreaker all check out against primary or authoritative sources. Required fixes before publishing: (1) remove the 'flat 7% indefinitely' alternative from the Ley 20.446 holiday description (closed 31 Dec 2025 for new entrants) and reword the UI 3.5 M route as still a tax-residency trigger that no longer unlocks the holiday; (2) replace Numbeo values with a dated edition (2025: QoL 139.8 / safety 48.0 / healthcare 68.6) and label FSI 33.7 as 2024; (3) add the 200/100-ha INC thresholds for Colonia/Florida/Maldonado/San José/Canelones and the 3-ha rural minimum in the five southern departments; (4) flag the '~90 companies / ~6 M ha', Artigas USD 2,300, mutualista fee ranges and USD 1,300/month figures as unverified estimates. With those edits the record is publishable.
